explanations: terra: “We raised the Mount above you” contrasts the section’s favorable لَكَ with a heavy object raised فَوْقَكُمْ while the people are charged to hold firmly to revelation.
terra: The repeated covenant scene again raises the Mount above the people, preserving the contrast between elevation as a threat over someone and elevation as honor for someone.
terra: A group given scripture casts God’s book behind their backs as if they did not know; revelation that can confer dhikr is instead put at the bodily place of deliberate dishonor.

luna: God tells Abraham He will make him a leader for people, then says His covenant does not reach wrongdoers. The section’s Abraham examples concern lasting honor; this passage gives him an explicit rank and a boundary on who can claim it.

luna: The section’s root ر ف ع includes literal raising as well as honor; Abraham and Ishmael raise the foundations of the House. This is a concrete physical use of the verb by Abraham, whose lasting name the section also discusses. | terra: Abraham and Ishmael raise the foundations of the House while praying for acceptance; physical raising of a sacred house prepares the more explicit meeting of raised houses and remembered divine name in 24:36.

luna: This verse says God chose Abraham in worldly life and counts him among the righteous in the Hereafter. It adds a direct divine judgment of Abraham’s standing to the section’s picture of his enduring, elevated name.

luna: The section’s root ذ ك ر includes remembrance as well as renown; here God says, “remember Me, I will remember you” (فاذكروني أذكركم). The reciprocity gives divine remembrance as a distinct form of favor alongside public praise.

luna: The section cites God’s raising some messengers by degrees (ورفع بعضهم درجات); this verse states that He raised some messengers above others in rank, directly locating divine elevation in prophetic status. | terra: Among the messengers, God speaks to some and “raises some of them by degrees,” directly applying رفع to differentiated prophetic rank.

luna: The section remembers God removing the Prophet’s burden; in this supplication believers ask, “do not place upon us a burden like that laid upon those before us” (ولا تحمل علينا إصرا كما حملته على الذين من قبلنا). It turns relief into a plea that such weight not be imposed. | terra: The believers ask God not to lay upon them a burden as He laid on earlier people and not to load them beyond capacity, a direct prayer for the relief enacted in the section.

luna: The section’s dictionary gloss for ر ف ع makes elevation the opposite of disgrace; this verse pairs God’s honoring whom He wills with humbling whom He wills (تعز من تشاء وتذل من تشاء), stating that boundary directly. | terra: God gives and removes dominion, honors whom He wills and humiliates whom He wills; divine elevation and ذِلَّة are presented as exact contrary changes of human standing.

luna: The section says 94:4 raises the Prophet’s remembrance rather than his person; in Jesus’s address God says, “I will raise you to Me” (ورافعك إلي). Whatever the mechanics of this raising, its grammatical object is Jesus himself, a person-directed counter-image. | terra: God tells Jesus, “I am raising you to Me” and purifying him from the disbelievers; here the person is raised, clarifying by contrast the section’s careful choice to raise the name.
terra: Those charged to make scripture known throw it behind their backs and trade it cheaply, reversing both public mention and honorable elevation of revealed speech.
terra: God desires to lighten for people because the human being was created weak, stating the mercy made visible when a back-breaking weight is reduced.

luna: The section’s secondary gloss for ظ ه ر describes a fault that does not attach to the innocent; this verse says one who casts a sin onto an innocent person bears slander and clear wrongdoing himself. It specifies where the blame and burden actually remain.
terra: God raises the Mount above the Children of Israel for their covenant; its object and “above them” relation clarify how much the object and preposition govern the value of رفع.
terra: “Rather, God raised him to Himself” again makes a prophet, rather than his mention, the grammatical object of رفع and thus exposes the section’s object distinction.

terra: After purification commands, God says He does not wish to place any hardship “upon you” but to purify and complete favor; it shares the motion of withholding a constricting load from the addressee.

luna: The section’s burden word وِزْر and the back ظَهْر meet their reversal at the Hour: deniers “carry their burdens on their backs” (يحملون أوزارهم على ظهورهم), making the back bear what 94 says was taken off it. | terra: Those who deny the meeting carry “their burdens upon their backs” (أَوْزَارَهُمْ عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ), the exact bodily counter-scene to the addressee’s burden being removed from his back.

luna: After Abraham’s argument against his people, the section cites the declaration “We raise by degrees whom We will” (نرفع درجات من نشاء). It makes rank a divine grant within the very Abraham narrative that frames the section’s comparison. | terra: After granting Abraham his argument, God says, “We raise by degrees whom We will,” making divinely given proof a means of elevated standing.

luna: The section’s opening-chest image has a direct reversal here: God opens a person’s chest to Islam, but makes another’s chest tight and constricted (يشرح صدره للإسلام ... يجعل صدره ضيقا حرجا). It shows the same inner capacity as both gift and deprivation. | terra: God opens the chest of one guided to submission but makes the chest of one led astray tight and constricted, as though climbing the sky; it supplies both the opening and its bodily reversal.

luna: In a passage insisting that each soul earns for itself, this verse repeats that no bearer bears another’s burden (ولا تزر وازرة وزر أخرى). It sharpens the section’s “from you” wording as a personal, not transferable, release. | terra: “No bearer bears the burden of another” fixes the possessive boundary implicit in “your burden”: guilt belongs to its bearer unless God removes it.

luna: The section’s root ر ف ع extends to rank; here people are made successors on earth and raised above one another in degrees as a test (ورفع بعضكم فوق بعض درجات ليبلوكم). The verse marks worldly elevation as an allotted trial, distinct from honor in remembrance. | terra: God makes people successors and raises some above others in degrees “to test you,” marking bestowed rank as responsibility rather than simple prestige.

luna: The section’s chest image and raised remembrance meet in this address about revelation: “let there be no tightness in your chest about it” (فلا يكن في صدرك حرج منه), then the verse calls the Book a reminder for believers (وذكرى للمؤمنين). It links the Prophet’s ease to the message he carries.

luna: The section’s verb و ض ع means setting something down, and 94:2 sets a burden off the Prophet; here the Messenger “removes from them their burden and shackles” (يضع عنهم إصرهم والأغلال), extending that concrete release to his followers. | terra: The unlettered Messenger is found written in earlier scripture, and he “puts off from them their burden” (يَضَعُ عَنْهُمْ إِصْرَهُمْ); his attested mention and the removal of a load meet in one ayah.

terra: God raises the mountain above the covenant people like a canopy and they think it will fall on them; the same divine “We raised” puts a massive weight overhead rather than raising a name for someone.

luna: The section’s dictionary gloss ر ف ع includes honor and height; here God says He could have raised a sign-bearer by the signs, but he clung to the earth (لرفعناه بها ولكنه أخلد إلى الأرض). It is a specific reversal of elevation into low attachment. | terra: God could have raised the man through His signs, but he clings to the earth and follows desire; divinely offered elevation is reversed by self-chosen abasement.
terra: The audience is asked whether they have reflected that there is no madness in their companion; sober recognition replaces the degrading label.
terra: “If they prevail over you” (إِن يَظْهَرُوا عَلَيْكُمْ) uses ظهر على in precisely the dictionary sense “overcome a person” developed in the section.

luna: The section’s dictionary branch for ظ ه ر includes prevailing over someone; here God sends the Messenger with guidance and the true religion “to make it prevail over all religion” (ليظهره على الدين كله), applying that root to public triumph. | terra: God sends the Messenger with guidance and the true religion “to make it prevail over every religion”; ظهر shifts from bodily back to publicly established ascendancy.
terra: In the cave scene the disbelievers’ word is made lowest while God’s word is highest, a nonlexical counterpart to lowering one thing and raising spoken mention.

luna: The section’s ṣ-d-r gloss includes the foremost part, and its horse reaches the finish first by its chest; this verse names the earliest forerunners among the migrants and helpers, then says God is pleased with them. It gives precedence a concrete communal honor.
terra: The Prophet’s chest is described as constricted by the opponents’ demand for treasure or an angel; their speech supplies a specific pressure answered by divine expansion and reassurance.
terra: The women confess that they know no evil of Joseph and the governor’s wife acknowledges his truthfulness, making an attached accusation fall away before his elevation.
terra: After Joseph’s vindication, the king declares him established and trusted; cleared blame is followed by publicly raised standing in the same narrative.

luna: In Joseph’s story, the section’s cited elevation formula recurs: “We raise by degrees whom We will” (نرفع درجات من نشاء). This places divinely granted rank within a scene of judgment and knowledge, broadening the image beyond public fame. | terra: In Joseph’s case God says, “We raise by degrees whom We will”; the elevation follows divinely given knowledge and vindication within the narrative.

luna: The section distinguishes a raised name from a raised person; Joseph seats his parents above him on the throne (ورفع أبويه على العرش), an explicit bodily elevation that sharpens that distinction. | terra: Joseph raises his parents upon the throne; literal placement above also publicly restores family dignity after his earlier abasement.

luna: The section joins an opened chest with the root ذ ك ر as remembrance and honor; this verse says hearts find rest through remembrance of God. It connects remembrance to an easing of the inner state, while using remembrance devotionally rather than as public renown.
terra: Mockers address the recipient of “the Reminder” and call him mad; the ayah stages the attempted attachment of disgrace to the very bearer of dhikr whose mention is raised.

luna: The section recalls the Prophet’s chest opened and burden removed; here God says He knows the Prophet’s chest tightens at what people say (يضيق صدرك بما يقولون). The shared addressee makes this a precise counter-scene of distress caused by speech. | terra: God tells the Prophet that He knows his chest is constricted by what they say; hostile speech narrows the same chest whose expansion and raised mention answer it in the section.

luna: The preceding 15:97 says the Prophet’s chest tightens at what people say; this verse’s own contribution is to command glorification and prostration (فسبح بحمد ربك وكن من الساجدين), placing praise beside that distress and echoing the section’s praise sense of ذ ك ر.
terra: Livestock carry people’s heavy loads to a land they could reach only with severe effort, supplying a literal carrier-and-weight scene against which relief from a human back can be felt.
terra: Misleaders bear their own burdens in full and some burdens of those they mislead, showing a load increased through responsibility rather than removed by grace.
terra: One who “opens his chest to disbelief” uses the same chest-opening form for the opposite moral reception, marking a boundary around expansion itself as an unqualified good.

luna: The section distinguishes the person from the weight on his back; this verse says each person’s lot is fastened to his neck and a record will be brought out. It offers a contrasting bodily image of accountability remaining attached to a person.

luna: The section’s burden word وِزْر is repeated in the rule that no bearer bears another’s burden (ولا تزر وازرة وزر أخرى); this verse sets that rule beside the sending of a messenger, so a burden is accountable to one’s own response to guidance. | terra: The same non-transfer rule appears in a passage on guidance and accountability, sharpening why removal of one addressee’s own وزر is exceptional mercy.

luna: The section’s “for you” raised remembrance is addressed to the Prophet; here God promises to raise him to a praised station (مقاما محمودا). The shared addressee and praise connect enduring honor with an elevated standing. | terra: The Prophet is promised that his Lord may raise him to “a praised station” (مَقَامًا مَّحْمُودًا), joining elevation of station to public praise.

luna: The section’s dictionary form ظهرت على الرجل means prevailing over someone; the youths fear that their people might prevail over them (إنهم إن يظهروا عليكم يرجموكم). It gives a concrete human conflict for the root’s “get above/overcome” sense. | terra: The sleepers warn that if their people “prevail over you” they will stone or reconvert them; ظهر على carries the developed dictionary sense of overcoming a person.

luna: The section’s dictionary gloss of ظ ه ر includes getting on top of something (ظهرت البيت علوته); this verse says the people could not climb over Dhul-Qarnayn’s barrier (فما اسطاعوا أن يظهروه), a concrete limit on rising above an obstacle. | terra: The peoples cannot “scale” the barrier (أَن يَظْهَرُوهُ), a Qur’anic use of ظهر in the section’s developed sense “to get on top of” something.

luna: The section’s raised-name image is echoed by God making for Abraham’s family “a lofty tongue of truth” (لسان صدق عليا). Here lasting truthful praise is granted to them, matching the section’s link between renown and honor. | terra: God gives Abraham and his descendants “a lofty tongue of truth” (لِسَانَ صِدْقٍ عَلِيًّا), a direct image of an honored and enduring good name granted “for them.”

luna: This verse tells the reader to remember Idris in the Book (واذكر في الكتاب إدريس); its own contribution is the act of textual remembrance, while the next verse, 19:57, says God raised him to a high place, bringing mention and elevation together. | terra: “Mention in the Book Idris” makes scriptural mention the action of this ayah; 19:57 then supplies its spatially raised counterpart.

luna: The section stresses that 94:4 raises the Prophet’s name, not his person; here God says He raised Idris to a high place (ورفعناه مكانا عليا). The bodily/person-directed wording provides a specific counter-image, while 19:56 first commands that Idris be remembered in the Book. | terra: “We raised him to a high place” uses the same first-person divine action as 94:4, while 19:56 has just placed Idris in remembered speech.

luna: The section describes a burden lifted from the Prophet; this address says the Quran was not sent down to make him miserable (ما أنزلنا عليك القرآن لتشقى), a direct statement of relief in the same prophetic address.

luna: The preceding 20:2 says the Quran was not sent to distress the Prophet; this verse’s own contribution is to call it a reminder (إلا تذكرة لمن يخشى), connecting the section’s lifted burden and raised ذ ك ر to the message’s purpose.

luna: Moses asks his Lord, “open my chest” (رب اشرح لي صدري), using the same chest image as 94:1. The petition places the opening in preparation for a difficult commission, while 94 recalls it as a granted favor. | terra: Moses prays, “My Lord, expand for me my chest” (ٱشْرَحْ لِي صَدْرِي), the closest repeated formulation of chest-opening with the same لِي relation.
terra: Moses’ next request, “make my task easy for me,” states the functional relief sought through the chest-opening of 20:25.
terra: Moses asks that Aaron strengthen his back/support (ٱشْدُدْ بِهِ أَزْرِي), so an opened chest is joined to a back made able to bear the prophetic task.

luna: The section treats ذ ك ر as something bestowed for the Prophet; after recounting earlier peoples, this verse says, “We have given you from Us a reminder” (وآتيناك من لدنا ذكرا), a direct parallel in speaker, recipient, and gift.

luna: The preceding 20:99 identifies the gift as a reminder; this verse’s own claim is that whoever turns away from it carries a burden on Judgment Day (فإنه يحمل يوم القيامة وزرا). It makes the section’s pairing of raised remembrance and removed weight consequential in the opposite direction. | terra: Whoever turns away from the divine reminder (ذِكْرِي) will carry a burden (وِزْرًا); rejection of dhikr produces the very load that the section sets opposite an elevated dhikr.
terra: This ayah continues 20:100 by making people abide under that burden and calling it an evil load on Resurrection Day, so the carried وزر is enduring rather than removed.

luna: The section cites the wording “a book in which is your remembrance” (فيه ذكركم) and notes that ذ ك ر can mean honor as well as recollection. The verse lets the Book carry the community’s remembrance, though that word may also mean admonition. | terra: God says He sent down a book “in which is your dhikr” (فِيهِ ذِكْرُكُمْ), making revealed speech the bearer of the community’s mention and standing.

luna: The section’s root و ض ع describes setting a burden down; at the Hour, this verse says every pregnant woman puts down her pregnancy. The shared bodily act makes the burden’s release concrete, though the verse’s scene is the terror of Judgment. | terra: At the Hour every pregnant one “lays down her load” (تَضَعُ كُلُّ ذَاتِ حَمْلٍ حَمْلَهَا); physical delivery supplies a bodily instance of وضع releasing a carried weight.

luna: The section defines elevation against humiliation; this verse says that one whom God humiliates has no one to honor him (ومن يهن الله فما له من مكرم). It makes divine elevation a status no human can confer against God’s judgment.

luna: The section’s opened chest presents inward capacity as a divine gift; this verse says it is hearts within chests that can become blind. That specific inward obstruction contrasts with the section’s opened capacity and grounds the image in perception.
terra: God has chosen the believers and placed no hardship upon them in religion; divine choosing is paired with refusing to put a constricting burden on them.
terra: The question “Do they say there is madness in him?” is answered by his bringing them the truth, opposing attempted degradation with the worth of his message.
terra: Those targeted by the slander are declared clear of what is said about them and promised forgiveness and noble provision, pairing non-adhering accusation with restored honor.

luna: The section joins its root ر ف ع, raising, to ذ ك ر, remembrance; this verse joins houses being raised with His name being mentioned in them (أن ترفع ويذكر فيها اسمه), picturing honor enacted in a place of worship. | terra: Houses are permitted “to be raised” and God’s name “to be mentioned” in them (تُرْفَعَ وَيُذْكَرَ فِيهَا ٱسْمُهُ); raising and mentioning a name are coordinated acts.
terra: Believers must not treat the Messenger’s summons among them like one another’s summons, a direct social boundary around how his call and address are honored.

luna: Moses says his chest is tight and his tongue will not flow (ويضيق صدري ولا ينطلق لساني), a concrete opposite to the section’s opened chest; the speech difficulty also makes bodily capacity relevant to a prophetic commission. | terra: Moses says his chest constricts and his tongue does not speak freely, the felt opposite of the chest-opening he asks for in 20:25 and receives in the section’s prophetic parallel.

luna: Abraham asks God to grant him “a tongue of truth among later generations” (لسان صدق في الآخرين); the prayer anticipates 19:50, where God grants his family a lofty tongue of truth, and makes enduring mention an explicitly requested favor. | terra: Abraham asks, “Make for me a tongue of truth among later people,” stating as a prayer the lasting honorable mention that the section says God raises for someone.
terra: Pharaoh exalts himself in the land and weakens one group of its people, an unethical counter-image in which self-elevation depends on pushing others down.

luna: The section pictures a weight so heavy it strains the Prophet’s back; this verse describes Qarun’s keys as heavy enough to burden a band of strong men. It supplies a literal load whose weight is visible through those trying to carry it.
terra: The final home is assigned to those who do not seek elevation on earth; it distinguishes status bestowed by God from self-sought عُلُوّ.

luna: The section’s burden is taken off one person; here those who mislead others are said to carry their own burdens plus additional burdens with them (وليحملن أثقالهم وأثقالا مع أثقالهم). It shows the opposite case where leading others astray adds weight to one’s account. | terra: The disbelievers will bear their own loads and additional loads with them, another explicit expansion of personal burden through misleading others.

luna: The section glosses ذ ك ر as renown and praise; this command for believers to invoke blessings on the Prophet gives a concrete communal practice of honoring him, though the verse describes blessings rather than raising his name. | terra: God and the angels bless the Prophet and believers are commanded to do likewise, giving a concrete, continually repeated form to his elevated mention.
terra: God clears Moses of what people said about him and he is distinguished in God’s sight; non-adhering blame and honored standing occur together exactly as in the section’s ظَهَرَ-based gloss.
terra: The Trust is offered to the heavens, earth, and mountains, which shrink from bearing it, while the human bears it; responsibility becomes a load whose acceptance can expose the bearer.
terra: After asking the audience to reflect, the ayah says there is no madness in their companion and identifies him as a warner, clearing defect and affirming office together.

luna: The section’s root ر ف ع includes elevating renown in speech; here good words ascend to God and righteous deeds raise them (إليه يصعد الكلم الطيب والعمل الصالح يرفعه). It makes verbal worth, not bodily height, the thing lifted. | terra: The ayah begins with all honor belonging to God, then says the good word ascends and righteous action raises it; honor, utterance, and upward motion form the section’s semantic equation.

luna: The section says the Prophet’s burden was set off him; this verse describes a burdened soul calling another to carry some, but none can carry it, even a close relative (وإن تدع مثقلة إلى حملها لا يحمل منه شيء ولو كان ذا قربى). It sets a boundary: removal of one person’s burden is not transfer to someone else. | terra: No bearer bears another’s burden, and if a heavily laden soul calls for help none of its load is carried; the ayah defines ownership and transfer of the load removed “from you.”

luna: This verse’s own contribution is that God saves Noah and his family from great distress; the same passage leaves a mention for Noah in 37:78 and greets him in 37:79. It brings relief from distress together with a lasting prophetic name, as the section does with the removed burden and raised remembrance.

luna: The section treats a raised name as lasting renown; here God says He leaves Noah remembered among later generations. The next verse’s peace upon Noah shows what that continuing mention looks like, while this ayah supplies the legacy claim itself. | terra: “We left for him among later generations” gives Noah an enduring posthumous mention, the same outcome Abraham requests as a truthful tongue among later people.

luna: The section describes remembrance as praise and renown; this verse’s own contribution is a peace greeting for Noah “among the worlds.” The preceding 37:78 says God left Noah remembered among later generations, completing the link between lasting mention and praise. | terra: “Peace upon Noah among all peoples” supplies the actual words of praise that 37:78 says were left for him.

luna: The section cites Abraham’s prayer for a truthful name among later generations; here the Quran says God left Abraham a mention among later people. The following verse’s greeting of peace on Abraham gives that renown a form of praise. | terra: “We left for him among later generations” realizes for Abraham the lasting mention requested in 26:84.

luna: This verse’s own contribution is a peace greeting for Abraham; 37:108 says God left him a mention among later generations. Together they give a specific Quranic form for the lasting honor the section associates with Abraham. | terra: “Peace upon Abraham” voices the honorable remembrance whose continuance 37:108 announces.

luna: The section links elevated remembrance to prophetic honor; this verse says God left Moses and Aaron a mention among later generations. The next verse’s peace upon both is the passage’s explicit honoring response. | terra: God leaves Moses and Aaron a remembrance among later generations, extending elevated mention to another prophetic pair.

luna: This verse greets Moses and Aaron with peace; the preceding 37:119 says God left them a mention among later generations. Its own contribution is an explicit praise formula attached to that legacy. | terra: “Peace upon Moses and Aaron” gives the praise preserved by the preceding ayah rather than merely asserting fame abstractly.

luna: The section’s raised-name image is repeated for Elijah: this verse says God left him a mention among later generations, and the next verse greets him with peace. Its own contribution is the continuing legacy claim. | terra: God leaves Elijah a remembrance among later generations, another direct instance of a divinely preserved name.

luna: This verse greets Elijah with peace; the preceding 37:129 says God left him a mention among later generations. It supplies the praise form that completes this repeated prophetic legacy pattern. | terra: “Peace upon Ilyasin” supplies the laudatory formula attached to the remembrance announced in 37:129.

luna: The section glosses ذ ك ر as honor and renown; the opening oath calls the Quran “possessor of remembrance” (ذي الذكر). If الذكر here means eminence, it directly parallels raised renown; if it means admonition, the connection is only the shared root. | terra: “The Qur’an endowed with dhikr” may carry the honor or renown sense of ذكر developed in the section, though “reminder” is also possible and makes this link uncertain.

luna: This verse repeats that no burden-bearer carries another’s burden (ولا تزر وازرة وزر أخرى) while saying God has no need of human disbelief; it frames the section’s personal burden as neither shared nor something God needs. | terra: “No burdened soul bears another’s burden” accompanies God’s knowledge of what is within breasts, linking accountable load and the inner person without transferring blame.

luna: Like the section’s opened chest, this verse describes a chest opened to Islam and then contrasts it with hearts hardened against God’s remembrance (شرح الله صدره للإسلام ... للقاسية قلوبهم من ذكر الله). It joins chest-capacity to the reception of remembrance. | terra: God’s opening of a person’s chest to submission places that person upon light from his Lord, making expanded chest an inward elevation and receptivity.

luna: The section’s root ر ف ع includes elevation of rank; this verse names God “Exalter of degrees” (رفيع الدرجات) and immediately describes revelation being sent to a chosen servant, giving elevation a divine source and prophetic setting. | terra: God is “Raiser of degrees” and sends the Spirit of His command upon whom He wills, bringing elevation of rank beside the choosing of a bearer of revelation.

luna: The section’s elevation vocabulary includes rank; this verse says God has raised some people above others in degrees (ورفعنا بعضهم فوق بعض درجات) while distributing livelihoods, showing social rank as differentiated provision rather than the Prophet’s raised renown. | terra: God raises some people above others in worldly degrees so they may employ one another, supplying a social and provisional sense of elevation distinct from prophetic honor.
terra: The imagined silver houses have stairways “on which they ascend” (عَلَيْهَا يَظْهَرُونَ), matching the section’s secondary ظهر sense of climbing onto a house.

luna: The section glosses its root ذ ك ر as fame and praise; the Quran calls this a remembrance “for you and your people” (لذكر لك ولقومك) and says they will be questioned about it, giving the Prophet’s elevated mention a communal horizon. | terra: The revelation is “a dhikr for you and your people” (لَذِكْرٌ لَّكَ وَلِقَوْمِكَ); ذِكْر and لَكَ repeat the section’s wording and present the revelation as their honor and renown.
terra: The mother carries her child with hardship and delivers it with hardship; حمل followed by وضع makes birth an embodied instance of laying down a painfully carried load.
terra: War itself finally “lays down its burdens” (تَضَعَ ٱلْحَرْبُ أَوْزَارَهَا), joining the section’s exact وضع and وزر terms in a second image of a crushing load being put off.

luna: The section does not say whether its burden is sin, so this remains uncertain; in the same direct address to the Prophet, God promises to forgive his earlier and later wrong (ليغفر لك الله ما تقدم من ذنبك وما تأخر). It offers a specific possible moral counterpart to a burden being removed.

luna: This verse repeats the section’s root-sense of prevailing: God sent His Messenger with guidance and the true religion “to make it prevail over all religion” (ليظهره على الدين كله). The repeated formulation gives the “rise over” sense a religious and public setting. | terra: The repeated promise that the Messenger’s true religion will be made prevailing over all religion gives public elevation to what he bears.
terra: Believers must not raise their voices above the Prophet’s voice; the physical act of رفع is bounded so that his social and prophetic standing is not violated.
terra: Those who lower their voices in the Messenger’s presence receive forgiveness and immense reward; the lowering that honors him completes the boundary set by 49:2.
terra: Those who call the Prophet from behind the private chambers are censured as lacking understanding, a concrete misuse of address that contrasts with his elevated social standing.

luna: The section’s dictionary gloss connects elevation with honor; this verse says the most honored before God is the most mindful, not a person’s lineage. It supplies a criterion for honor that distinguishes divine worth from inherited status.
terra: “Remind, for by your Lord’s favor you are neither soothsayer nor mad” couples the Prophet’s act of reminding with the removal of two public stigmas.

luna: The section names the Prophet’s burden as وِزْر; this passage states that no burden-bearer carries another’s burden (ألا تزر وازرة وزر أخرى), making personal responsibility the boundary around the burden removed from him. | terra: The scrolls of Moses and Abraham state that no bearer bears another’s burden, placing the load’s personal ownership within older prophetic teaching.

luna: The section defines roots و ض ع and ر ف ع as opposites; this verse uses both in one ordered scene, raising the heaven and setting down the balance (والسماء رفعها ووضع الميزان). The different objects clarify how opposed motions can serve distinct purposes. | terra: God “raised” the heaven and “set down” the balance (رَفَعَهَا وَوَضَعَ ٱلْمِيزَانَ), bringing the section’s expressly opposed verbs together while keeping their objects distinct.
terra: “The earth He laid down for creatures” gives وضع a spatial object below, completing the raised heaven of 55:7 and sharpening the section’s vertical opposition.

luna: The section pairs lowering a burden with raising a name; this verse describes the Event as lowering and raising (خافضة رافعة). Its reversal makes status unstable at judgment, unlike the specific favor of the Prophet’s enduring mention. | terra: The Event is “lowering, raising” (خَافِضَةٌ رَّافِعَةٌ), compressing the same reversal of rank into two opposed participles.

luna: The section’s dictionary gloss ص د ر includes the foremost part, and its horse example reaches the finish first by its chest; this verse identifies “the foremost” (والسابقون السابقون). It gives a nonlexical Quranic parallel between being first and elevated standing. | terra: “The foremost, the foremost” turns precedence into a named class, recalling the section’s horse that arrives ahead by its chest.
terra: “These are the ones brought near” supplies the elevated rank that follows the precedence announced in 56:10.

luna: The section’s ص د ر dictionary example describes a horse taking the lead with its chest; this verse tells people to race toward forgiveness and a garden (سابقوا إلى مغفرة من ربكم وجنة). The Quran applies forward precedence to seeking divine reward.

luna: The section’s dictionary gloss ص د ر includes the head place of an assembly, and its root ر ف ع includes raising in rank; after believers make room in gatherings, this verse says God raises believers and knowledge-holders by degrees (يرفع الله ... درجات), joining the two details. | terra: After commands governing room and rising in assemblies, God raises believers and people of knowledge by degrees; the section’s dictionary image of the head of a مجلس becomes moral rank here.

luna: The section’s raised-name image concerns a Prophet known beyond his own time; Jesus announces a messenger after him by name (اسمه أحمد). This is a specific case of a prophetic identity transmitted through earlier speech, not an explicit statement that the name is raised. | terra: Jesus announces a messenger to come after him “whose name is Ahmad,” giving the future Prophet an honorable name voiced before his own community appears.

luna: The section’s dictionary branch for ظ ه ر includes prevailing over another; this verse again says the Messenger was sent with guidance and truth “to make it prevail over all religion” (ليظهره على الدين كله), a public triumph sense rather than bodily elevation. | terra: This third formulation of making the Messenger’s religion prevail preserves the section’s developed ظهر sense of overcoming, now applied to revealed truth.
terra: After God strengthens the believers against their enemy, they become “prevailing” (ظَاهِرِينَ), another Qur’anic realization of the section’s ظهر sense of ascendancy.
terra: The donkey carrying books pictures revelation borne merely as weight rather than received as honor or guidance, reversing the section’s book-as-dhikr and load-removed relations.

luna: The section defines elevation as honor and its opposite as humiliation; this verse answers a boast that the more honored would expel the more humble by stating that honor belongs to God, His Messenger, and believers. It places the Prophet’s honor under God’s grant rather than human status claims. | terra: Honor belongs to God, His Messenger, and the believers; the Messenger’s standing is expressly placed on the side of عِزَّة rather than the section’s ذِلَّة.
terra: The waiting term lasts until pregnant women “lay down their load,” another exact use of وضع for bodily release from something carried.
terra: God directly tells the Prophet that, by his Lord’s favor, he is not mad; a publicly alleged defect is kept from adhering to the addressee.
terra: The same address then declares the Prophet to be upon tremendous character, replacing the rejected stigma of 68:2 with explicit praise.

luna: The section does not identify the Prophet’s burden with revelation, so this is only a possible parallel: God says He will cast upon him a “heavy word” (قولا ثقيلا). It makes prophetic speech a weighty commission, without defining the burden of 94:2. | terra: God tells the same prophetic addressee that He will cast “a weighty word” upon him; a heavy charge placed عَلَيْكَ supplies the counter-motion to a burden later taken عَنكَ.
terra: “Your companion is not mad” rejects an accusation against the Messenger in the audience’s own relational language, another case of blame failing to adhere.

luna: The section’s chest-of-the-horse gloss makes first place visible as a race; this verse says that for the lasting reward, competitors should compete (وفي ذلك فليتنافس المتنافسون), a specific moral contest rather than a claim about bodily rank.
terra: Receiving one’s record from behind the back marks humiliation and impending ruin, a bodily counter-image to the section’s back relieved and name honored.

luna: This verse reports a person reading abundant provision as proof that God has honored him; the next two verses give the opposite reading and reject the inference. Its own contribution is the first mistaken equation of provision with honor, a useful boundary for the section’s raised-name image.

luna: This verse reports a person reading restricted provision as humiliation; 89:15 supplies the opposite claim, and 89:17 corrects both. Its own contribution shows that hardship does not itself mean the person has been lowered.

luna: This verse rejects the preceding claims that abundance means honor and scarcity means humiliation, then points to failure to honor the orphan. It clarifies that the section’s elevation of a name is honor, not merely a material condition.
terra: God tells the same prophetic addressee that his Lord has neither forsaken nor detested him, explicitly preventing the disgrace implied by hostile or anxious speech from adhering.
terra: “The Hereafter is better for you than the first” follows the denial of abandonment and uses لَكَ to promise an ascending valuation of the Prophet’s future.
terra: The Lord promises to give the Prophet until he is pleased, completing 93:3–4 with positive divine favor after rejected disgrace.

luna: The section’s root ذ ك ر includes public mention and praise; this command tells the Prophet to speak of his Lord’s blessing. The connection is indirect because the verse publicizes God’s favor rather than the Prophet’s name, but it gives a specific response to bestowed favor.

terra: God then returns the human being to the lowest of the low; here the person himself is lowered, illuminating the section’s insistence that its lowered object is the burden rather than the person.

luna: The section’s burden is removed from a person; at the final shaking, this verse says the earth casts out its loads. It transfers the image to the earth itself and makes discharged weight an end-time scene.
terra: The divine gift of abundance to the Prophet supplies the positive grant whose opposite side is the hater’s being cut off in 108:3.
terra: The Prophet’s hater is “the one cut off,” a specific reversal of lasting mention: the opponent expects the Prophet’s name to end, but the severance is assigned to the opponent.
